1kc4nis: To describe a house in Spanish you need three verbs: **hay**, **estar**, and **ser**. They are not interchangeable: each one answers a different question. This week you learn to choose well, and to use **estar** for states: tired, happy, dirty, open…
b8dsrz: Hay, estar, and ser: three questions, three verbs
2lmfib: **Hay** answers the question _¿qué hay?_ (what is there?): it introduces something for the first time, it says it exists. **Hay dos dormitorios. Hay un balcón. No hay ascensor.** After _hay_ comes a number, **un / una / unos / unas**, or a noun without an article. Never _el_ or _la_.
142ny6f: **Estar** answers _¿dónde está?_ (where is it?): it gives the location of something we already know. That's why it takes **el, la, mi, tu…** before it: **El apartamento está en el centro. La cocina está al lado de la sala. Mi cuarto está en el segundo piso.**
13n575i: **Ser** answers _¿cómo es?_ (what is it like?): it describes the characteristics that are part of the thing. **El apartamento es grande. Es moderno. Es de alquiler.** It is also used to identify: **Esta es la cocina.**
1l0eubn: A natural description uses all three verbs together: **Mi casa está en un barrio tranquilo. Es pequeña, pero es muy bonita. Hay una sala, una cocina y dos cuartos.**
v7tzmj: Look at the article: **un / una** or a number → almost always _hay_; **el / la / mi** + place → almost always _está_.
1idmx6o: _La cocina_ is already known (it takes _la_): for its location we use **está**, not _hay_.
70t5nt: _Un baño_ is new information: we use **hay**.
rrtib9: Estar + adjective: how you are, how the house is
drye95: With **estar** + adjective we say the **state** of a person or thing at a specific moment: **Estoy cansada. Estamos contentos. La cocina está sucia. La farmacia está cerrada.**
5h9amn: With **ser** + adjective we say what something is normally like: its characteristic. Compare: **La cocina es pequeña** (always, it's its size) and **La cocina está sucia** (today; tomorrow it may be clean).
13yt9kb: The adjective agrees with the person or thing in gender and number: **La ventana está abierta. Los cuartos están ordenados. Ana y Luz están cansadas.**
j5jzlb: Very useful state adjectives. For people: **cansado, contento, nervioso, enfermo, aburrido, ocupado**. For things and places: **limpio, sucio, ordenado, desordenado, abierto, cerrado, roto, libre**.
1dq8vaz: If you can add **hoy** or **ahora** and the sentence makes sense, you probably need **estar**: _Hoy la casa está desordenada._
ylgvd8: _Abierta_ is a state (right now): it goes with **estar**.
3xrlxm: How you feel today is a state: **estoy**.
sabv6d: Parts of the house and floors
i8htou: Words for the house change by country. A dwelling in a building is a **piso** in Spain, an **apartamento** in Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, or the Caribbean, and a **departamento** in Mexico, Argentina, Chile, or Peru. The room for sleeping is the **dormitorio**, the **habitación**, or the **cuarto**; in Mexico, also the **recámara**. The living room is the **salón** in Spain and the **sala** in Latin America.
1s9p90f: For the number of the floor we use ordinals: **primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto, sexto, séptimo, octavo, noveno, décimo**. Before a masculine noun, _primero_ and _tercero_ lose the **-o**: **el primer piso, el tercer piso**. With a feminine noun they agree: **la primera planta, la tercera puerta**.
wydkrp: Careful: in Spain, the street level is the **planta baja** and the **primer piso** is above it. In many Latin American countries, the **primer piso** is the street level. When you are not sure, ask: **¿Es el piso de la calle?**
pra2jv: _Planta_ is feminine: **primera**. Only the masculine loses the -o.

vdv2mx: Last week you linked consonant + vowel (los_amigos). This week we link **vowel + vowel**. When a word ends in a vowel and the next one begins with a vowel, the two vowels go in the **same syllable**. It's called **sinalefa** (synalepha): _la amiga_ doesn't sound "la · a-mi-ga," but **la_a-mi-ga**, with three beats.
qpgpnd: The **h** is silent, so there is also synalepha in **mi_hijo**, **la_habitación**, **su_hermano**: the vowels touch.
1f5ab11: If the two vowels are the same, they almost merge into one, a little longer: **está_abierta**, **la_amiga**. If they are different, you go from one to the other without stopping: **mi_apartamento**, **todo_está**.
17mfnqd: That's why Spanish sounds so continuous: within a sentence there are no pauses between words, and each syllable lasts about the same. If you separate each word, your Spanish sounds slow and choppy.
15iu5fw: In Caribbean speech, also in Panama, the final **-s** is often aspirated or disappears (_los amigos_ → "loh amigo"). That's why even more vowels appear together there. You don't need to imitate it, but it's good to recognize it.
1i5k4x9: Synalepha is not written: the space between words is still there, but you don't hear it. The initial **h** is also silent, so it doesn't prevent the link: _la_habitación_.
